title: Weaver, shoemaker, barber, king
hookLine: the Bhagats' trades read like a street; that's the point

lines: LEATHER, A RAZOR, A MUDDY FARMER.
A PALACE AT THE END OF THE ROAD.
cards: A clatter from a loom in a doorway. Next door, someone bent over a shoe, stitching leather. Further on, a barber with a razor and a customer half-shaved.
A farmer coming in from the fields with mud on his feet. And at the end of the road, a palace.
Walk the names of the Bhagats in the Guru Granth Sahib and that's the street you're walking down: weaver, shoemaker, barber, king.

teach.h: IN THEIR OWN WORDS: LOOM, PRINT, CATTLE.
teach.b: Some of these trades come from the Bhagats' own mouths. Kabir calls himself a weaver in his hymns, and works the loom into his songs. Namdev says he was born in the house of a calico printer.
Ravidas says his family carried the dead cattle, work the caste order of his day looked down on.
Others come from tradition: Sain the barber, Dhanna the farmer, Pipa the king who gave up his throne. Side by side, they don't read like a list of holy men from one class. They read like a street.
That's the point. Ravidas's own hymns show a town that ranked people by birth, where a leather-worker's touch was counted as polluting.

The Granth answers by putting the weaver's song, the leather-worker's song and the king's song on the same pages, in the same raags, under the same honor. The barber's hymn is sung with the same reverence as the king's.

Guru Nanak says it in his own words in Raag Asa, in paraphrase: recognize the light in everyone, and don't ask about caste; in the world beyond, there is no caste. So the mix of trades isn't decoration.

You can't hold the Guru Granth Sahib in your hands and keep the street out of it. And it runs both ways: the king isn't shut out either. Pipa's place there is as a devotee, beside the others, not above them.

how: Sikhs point to the Bhagats' different trades and castes as part of the Guru Granth Sahib's teaching that birth sets no limit on devotion, and the langar, where all sit together, puts the same teaching into practice.

o: one who stitches shoes from leather
one who works a loom, as Kabir did
one who dyes and prints calico cloth

games.q: who worked where — tap the pairs.
p: born in a calico printer's house
his family carried the dead cattle

s: the Bhagats in the Granth all came from one class
their trades read like a street: weaver, printer, leather worker, barber, farmer, king.
some Bhagats name their own trades in their hymns
Kabir the weaver, Namdev the calico printer's son, Ravidas whose family carried dead cattle.
the king's hymn is placed above the others
Pipa's place is as a devotee, beside the others, not above them.

games.q: you're gathering holy songs, and the best ones come from a weaver, a leather worker and a barber. birth is supposed to shut them out. what do you do?
o: keep only the songs by the high-born.
keep the songs but hide who wrote them.
keep them, under their own names, beside everyone else's.
games.why: the Granth keeps their songs under their own names, in the same raags and with the same honor; the mix is the teaching.

practice: Walk your own street in your mind: whoever drives the bus, stacks the shelves, cuts hair, answers the phone, runs the office. Picture their faces as clearly as you can, each one a name on the same page.
If you pray, let Waheguru go with each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Weaver. Kabir's own word for himself, at the head of a street of Bhagats: weaver, printer, leather worker, barber, farmer, king.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: a devotee; the Granth's name for these poets from every trade.

carryVoice: Your line: the whole street. Loom, razor, field and palace, on the same pages. Day seven hundred ninety-six, done.
